title: Five forms (CCC 2626–2643)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary prays: her fiat, be it done to me, and her Magnificat. Your line was yes, then praise. What did you say yes to? Today closes the week. Day one thousand one hundred forty-one.

One kitchen, one ordinary day, two people who love each other. Good morning, glad you're here. Could you grab milk on the way home? Call your sister, she's having a hard week. Thank you for dinner. And once, out of nowhere: you're amazing, you know that? Greeting, asking, asking for someone else, thanks, and plain admiration. Nobody learns those as categories. They're just what love sounds like. The Catechism names the same shapes in prayer. Today: the five forms.
screen: `GOOD MORNING. COULD YOU GRAB MILK?` → `CALL YOUR SISTER.` → `THANK YOU. YOU'RE AMAZING.`

segments.voice: First, blessing and adoration. Blessing, the Catechism says, is a meeting of God and the person: God blesses, and the heart blesses back the one who is the source of every blessing. Adoration is the creature standing before the Creator, and knowing it. Second, petition: asking. The Catechism says asking shows we know what we are: creatures, not our own beginning. We ask because we need. And it says the first thing to ask for is forgiveness, and then the kingdom, before anything else. Third, intercession: asking for someone else. The Catechism says this is what Jesus does for us, and that Christian intercession has no boundaries. It reaches even enemies. Fourth, thanksgiving. The Catechism says every event and every need can become an offering of thanks, and quotes Saint Paul in the Douay-Rheims: "In all things give thanks." It also ties thanksgiving to the Eucharist, whose Greek name means thanksgiving. Fifth, praise. Here the Catechism draws a fine line. Praise, it says, gives God glory for his own sake, beyond anything he does, simply because he is. Thanks answers a gift; praise, in that picture, asks for nothing. And the Catechism says the Eucharist gathers all of them into one. Now the week. The ninth commandment: they shall see God. The tenth: enough. Then Part Four opened. What prayer is: God thirsts that we thirst. Old Testament prayer: the long school. Jesus prays: he prayed first. Mary prays: yes, then praise. And today, five forms, five ways to speak.
screen: `BLESSING AND ADORATION.` · `PETITION, THEN INTERCESSION.` · `THANKSGIVING: IN ALL THINGS.` · `PRAISE: FOR WHO GOD IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray all five, briefly. Settle, and breathe. Take each one for a few breaths, in your own words. Blessing: notice where you're standing, before something larger than you. Petition: name one thing you need. Intercession: name one person who needs something. Thanksgiving: name one thing from today. Praise: if you pray, say something to God that asks for nothing at all. If you don't pray, walk through the five as ways of paying attention. The bell holds the time.
Five forms. Blessing and adoration, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, and praise: in Catholic teaching, the shapes prayer takes, all gathered into the Eucharist. Today's word.
Your line: five ways to speak. Today, notice which of the five you use most, and give one of the others a turn. Day one thousand one hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: The Mass holds the forms of prayer together: praise in the Gloria, petition and intercession in the prayers of the faithful, and thanksgiving in the Eucharistic Prayer.

notes: CCC paraphrased throughout (copyrighted translation). Check: blessing as encounter and adoration as the creature's first attitude (2626–2628); petition, asking forgiveness first, then the kingdom (2629–2632); intercession with no boundaries, even enemies (2634–2636); thanksgiving and the Eucharist, 1 Thess 5:18 (2637–2638); praise for God's own sake (2639); the Eucharist containing all forms (2643).

'Praise, in that picture, asks for nothing': CCC 2639 says praise is the form of prayer that recognizes most immediately that God is God and gives him glory for his own sake; the script says only that praise asks for nothing. Confirm.
'The Eucharist, whose Greek name means thanksgiving' follows CCC 1328 and 2637; confirm.

Editor: praise line now follows CCC 2639 (glory for God's own sake, beyond what he does) rather than an unsourced thanks/praise rule, in voice, myth and fork; CCC 1328 added to sources for the Eucharist-means-thanksgiving line.
Editor (second pass): hook recast as a scene in the third person so it no longer directs the listener ('listen to the way you talk', 'nobody taught you').

Audit (1132–1141 pass): 'the Catechism calls it natural' (not in CCC 2629) replaced with CCC 2629's own point, that petition expresses awareness that we are creatures who are not our own beginning; 1 Thessalonians 5:18 (Douay-Rheims) and CCC 2626–2643 checked and found accurate.
